## Solution

We seek the unique holomorphic $V$ on $\{z:|z|>1\}$ satisfying $V(z^2)=2zV(z)+1$.

### Ansatz

Seek $V$ vanishing at $\infty$: $V(z)=\sum_{n\ge 1}a_n z^{-n}$, converging for $|z|>1$ (so $V(\infty)=0$). Substituting:

$$V(z^2)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n z^{-2n},\qquad 2zV(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}2a_n z^{1-n}.$$

Setting $V(z^2)-2zV(z)=1$ and matching the coefficient of $z^{-m}$ ($m\ge0$):

$$\bigl[m\text{ even}: a_{m/2}\bigr]-2a_{m+1}=\delta_{m,0}.$$

- $m=0$: $a_0-2a_1=1$; with $a_0=0$: $a_1=-\tfrac12$.
- $m\ge1$: $a_{m+1}=\tfrac12\,a_{m/2}$ if $m$ even, and $a_{m+1}=0$ if $m$ odd.

Equivalently, for $n\ge1$: $a_n=0$ if $n$ even; $a_n=\tfrac12 a_{(n-1)/2}$ if $n$ odd. Starting from $a_1=-\tfrac12$:

$$a_1=-2^{-1},\quad a_3=-2^{-2},\quad a_7=-2^{-3},\quad a_{15}=-2^{-4},\quad\dots$$

and every other $a_n$ vanishes. By induction $a_{2^k-1}=-2^{-k}$ ($k\ge1$) and $a_n=0$ otherwise. Hence

$$\boxed{\,V(z)=-\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}\,z^{\,1-2^k}=-\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^k\,z^{\,2^k-1}}\,}.$$

### Convergence and holomorphicity

For $|z|\ge r>1$, the $k$-th term is bounded by $2^{-k}r^{1-2^k}=2^{-k}r\cdot r^{-2^k}$, which is summable (super-exponential decay in $k$). By the Weierstrass $M$-test the series converges absolutely and uniformly on compact subsets of $\{|z|>1\}$, so $V$ is holomorphic there.

### Verification of the functional equation

$$V(z^2)=-\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}z^{2-2^{k+1}}\xrightarrow{j=k+1}-\sum_{j\ge2}2^{1-j}z^{2-2^j}.$$

$$2zV(z)+1=1-\sum_{k\ge1}2^{1-k}z^{2-2^k}=1-2^{0}z^{0}-\sum_{k\ge2}2^{1-k}z^{2-2^k}=-\sum_{k\ge2}2^{1-k}z^{2-2^k}.$$

These agree, so $V(z^2)=2zV(z)+1$. ✓

### Uniqueness

Let $W=V_1-V_2$ be the difference of two holomorphic solutions on $|z|>1$; then $W(z^2)=2zW(z)$. The Laurent series of $W$ converges in the annulus $1<|z|<\infty$, so it splits as

$$W(z)=\underbrace{\sum_{n\ge0}d_n z^n}_{f(z)\text{ (entire)}}+\underbrace{\sum_{n\ge1}b_n z^{-n}}_{g(z)\text{ (holomorphic on }|z|>1,\ g(\infty)=0)}.$$

Substituting into $W(z^2)=2zW(z)$ and rearranging:

$$f(z^2)-2zf(z)=2zg(z)-g(z^2)=:R(z).$$

The left side is entire. As $z\to\infty$, $g(z)=b_1/z+O(z^{-2})$ gives $2zg(z)\to2b_1$ and $g(z^2)\to0$, so $R(z)\to2b_1$; thus $R$ is bounded near $\infty$. Since $R$ agrees with the entire function $f(z^2)-2zf(z)$ on $|z|>1$, that entire function is bounded near $\infty$, hence bounded on all of $\mathbb C$ (continuous on the compact disk $|z|\le R$), and by Liouville is the constant $2b_1$:

$$f(z^2)-2zf(z)=2b_1.$$

Writing $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}d_nz^n$ and comparing coefficients:
- $z^0$: $d_0=2b_1$; $\ z^1$: $0=2d_0\Rightarrow d_0=0\Rightarrow b_1=0$;
- $z^{2n+1}$ ($n\ge0$): $0=2d_{2n}\Rightarrow d_{2n}=0$ for all $n$;
- $z^{2n}$ ($n\ge1$): $d_n=2d_{2n-1}$, i.e. $d_{2n-1}=d_n/2$.

With $d_1=2d_1\Rightarrow d_1=0$ and $d_{2n-1}=d_n/2$ (lower index $(n)$, already zero by induction since $(n)<(2n-1)$ for $n>1$), every $d_m=0$. So $f\equiv0$ and $b_1=0$.

It remains that $g(z^2)=2zg(z)$ with $g(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_nz^{-n}$, $g(\infty)=0$. Matching coefficients of $z^{-m}$:
- $z^0$: $0=2b_1\Rightarrow b_1=0$;
- $m\ge1$: $b_{m+1}=0$ if $m$ odd; $b_{m+1}=\tfrac12 b_{m/2}$ if $m$ even.

By strong induction $b_n=0$ for all $n$ (if $m+1$ even, the odd case gives it directly; if $m+1$ odd, $b_{m+1}=\tfrac12 b_{(m+1-1)/2}=\tfrac12 b_{m/2}=0$ by the induction hypothesis since $m/2<m+1$). Hence $g\equiv0$, so $W\equiv0$.

Therefore the solution is unique. $\blacksquare$

## Solution

We seek the unique holomorphic $V$ on $\{z:|z|>1\}$ satisfying $V(z^2)=2zV(z)+1$.

### Ansatz

Seek $V$ vanishing at $\infty$: $V(z)=\sum_{n\ge 1}a_n z^{-n}$, converging for $|z|>1$ (so $V(\infty)=0$). Substituting:

$$V(z^2)=\sum_{n\ge1}a_n z^{-2n},\qquad 2zV(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}2a_n z^{1-n}.$$

Setting $V(z^2)-2zV(z)=1$ and matching the coefficient of $z^{-m}$ ($m\ge0$):

$$\bigl[m\text{ even}: a_{m/2}\bigr]-2a_{m+1}=\delta_{m,0}.$$

- $m=0$: $a_0-2a_1=1$; with $a_0=0$: $a_1=-\tfrac12$.
- $m\ge1$: $a_{m+1}=\tfrac12\,a_{m/2}$ if $m$ even, and $a_{m+1}=0$ if $m$ odd.

Equivalently, for $n\ge1$: $a_n=0$ if $n$ even; $a_n=\tfrac12 a_{(n-1)/2}$ if $n$ odd. Starting from $a_1=-\tfrac12$:

$$a_1=-2^{-1},\quad a_3=-2^{-2},\quad a_7=-2^{-3},\quad a_{15}=-2^{-4},\quad\dots$$

and every other $a_n$ vanishes. By induction $a_{2^k-1}=-2^{-k}$ ($k\ge1$) and $a_n=0$ otherwise. Hence

$$\boxed{\,V(z)=-\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}\,z^{\,1-2^k}=-\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^k\,z^{\,2^k-1}}\,}.$$

### Convergence and holomorphicity

For $|z|\ge r>1$, the $k$-th term is bounded by $2^{-k}r^{1-2^k}=2^{-k}r\cdot r^{-2^k}$, which is summable (super-exponential decay in $k$). By the Weierstrass $M$-test the series converges absolutely and uniformly on compact subsets of $\{|z|>1\}$, so $V$ is holomorphic there.

### Verification of the functional equation

$$V(z^2)=-\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}z^{2-2^{k+1}}\xrightarrow{j=k+1}-\sum_{j\ge2}2^{1-j}z^{2-2^j}.$$

$$2zV(z)+1=1-\sum_{k\ge1}2^{1-k}z^{2-2^k}=1-2^{0}z^{0}-\sum_{k\ge2}2^{1-k}z^{2-2^k}=-\sum_{k\ge2}2^{1-k}z^{2-2^k}.$$

These agree, so $V(z^2)=2zV(z)+1$. ✓

### Uniqueness

Let $W=V_1-V_2$ be the difference of two holomorphic solutions on $|z|>1$; then $W(z^2)=2zW(z)$. The Laurent series of $W$ converges in the annulus $1<|z|<\infty$, so it splits as

$$W(z)=\underbrace{\sum_{n\ge0}d_n z^n}_{f(z)\text{ (entire)}}+\underbrace{\sum_{n\ge1}b_n z^{-n}}_{g(z)\text{ (holomorphic on }|z|>1,\ g(\infty)=0)}.$$

Substituting into $W(z^2)=2zW(z)$ and rearranging:

$$f(z^2)-2zf(z)=2zg(z)-g(z^2)=:R(z).$$

The left side is entire. As $z\to\infty$, $g(z)=b_1/z+O(z^{-2})$ gives $2zg(z)\to2b_1$ and $g(z^2)\to0$, so $R(z)\to2b_1$; thus $R$ is bounded near $\infty$. Since $R$ agrees with the entire function $f(z^2)-2zf(z)$ on $|z|>1$, that entire function is bounded near $\infty$, hence bounded on all of $\mathbb C$ (continuous on the compact disk $|z|\le R$), and by Liouville is the constant $2b_1$:

$$f(z^2)-2zf(z)=2b_1.$$

Writing $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}d_nz^n$ and comparing coefficients:
- $z^0$: $d_0=2b_1$; $\ z^1$: $0=2d_0\Rightarrow d_0=0\Rightarrow b_1=0$;
- $z^{2n+1}$ ($n\ge0$): $0=2d_{2n}\Rightarrow d_{2n}=0$ for all $n$;
- $z^{2n}$ ($n\ge1$): $d_n=2d_{2n-1}$, i.e. $d_{2n-1}=d_n/2$.

With $d_1=2d_1\Rightarrow d_1=0$ and $d_{2n-1}=d_n/2$ (lower index $(n)$, already zero by induction since $(n)<(2n-1)$ for $n>1$), every $d_m=0$. So $f\equiv0$ and $b_1=0$.

It remains that $g(z^2)=2zg(z)$ with $g(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_nz^{-n}$, $g(\infty)=0$. Matching coefficients of $z^{-m}$:
- $z^0$: $0=2b_1\Rightarrow b_1=0$;
- $m\ge1$: $b_{m+1}=0$ if $m$ odd; $b_{m+1}=\tfrac12 b_{m/2}$ if $m$ even.

By strong induction $b_n=0$ for all $n$ (if $m+1$ even, the odd case gives it directly; if $m+1$ odd, $b_{m+1}=\tfrac12 b_{(m+1-1)/2}=\tfrac12 b_{m/2}=0$ by the induction hypothesis since $m/2<m+1$). Hence $g\equiv0$, so $W\equiv0$.

Therefore the solution is unique. $\blacksquare$
